HB 36 tightens the rules governing how Alaska places foster children in psychiatric settings and reshapes requirements for treatment foster homes. The bill amends statutes on foster care placement to restrict or condition when a child in state custody can be placed in a hospital or residential psychiatric treatment center, sets specific duties for the Department of Family and Community Services (DFCS) regarding those placements, and addresses oversight and care requirements for children sent to psychiatric residential treatment facilities (PRTFs) outside Alaska. It also amends Rule 12.1(b) of the Alaska Child in Need of Aid Rules of Procedure, adjusting court procedure connected to these placements.

Neither the Department of Health (DOH) nor DFCS submitted analytical text with their blue sheets, and both declined to make a formal recommendation. As a result, no agency fiscal estimates, implementation concerns, or interagency disagreements are on record from those submissions. The absence of blue-sheet analysis means the Governor's office cannot draw on departmental views about cost, operational feasibility, or legal risk from these sources alone.

The bill's practical reach is significant: it touches placement decisions affecting some of Alaska's most vulnerable children, modifies inter-agency responsibilities split between DOH and DFCS following their recent separation, and extends to out-of-state facility placements where oversight has historically been limited. Without substantive agency input in the available record, the precise fiscal and operational implications remain unquantified.
